title: S'pore woman sues private-hire driver for braking when chicken crossed road, loses suit & ordered to pay S$15,000
text:
S'pore woman sues private-hire driver for braking when chicken crossed road, loses suit & ordered to pay S$15,000 - Mothership.SG - News from Singapore, Asia and around the world

Court
 S'pore woman sues private-hire driver for braking when chicken crossed road, loses suit & ordered to pay S$15,000
 The judge said the incident was part of the vicissitudes of life.
 Khine Zin Htet 
 November 19, 2026, 05:58 PM
Photo from Canva
 When a chicken crossed the road along Holland Road, a private-hire driver braked to avoid colliding with the vehicle in front, which had similarly braked. 
 The passenger in the driver's car later sued him for negligence, saying the incident caused her to suffer personal injuries. 
 In a judgment on Nov. 18, the judge dismissed the passenger's case and ordered her to pay S$15,000 in costs. 
 While he acknowledged that the woman was an innocent passenger who was injured in an incident which she had no control over, he noted that "the law does not seek out a tortfeasor for every loss that is suffered". 
 "In an imperfect world, some losses must lie where they fall. This incident, caused as it was by a chicken crossing the road, was unfortunately, but also undoubtedly, part of the vicissitudes of life," he said. 
 Incident
 The passenger, Yvonne Chen Qianyun, was in a private-hire vehicle driven by Tan Teng Kiat along Holland Road on Feb. 19, 2024. 
 When a chicken encroached into the path of the vehicle in front of Tan's vehicle, he applied his brakes to avoid a collision. 
 Chen claimed that this caused her to suffer personal injuries. 
 She mainly argued her case on the point that Tan failed to keep an adequate following distance. 
 Chen claimed that the force and manner of his braking exceeded what was "reasonably necessary to avoid a collision", saying that Tan had breached the standard of care required of him. 
 Tan agreed that he owed a duty of care to Chen but maintained that given his speed and his distance from the vehicle in front, he had sufficient distance and time to brake. 
 He therefore only needed to apply a “normal” brake instead of an "emergency or hard brake". 
 Other points of consideration
 The judge also noted that after the incident, Chen had asked Tan if he had noted the licence plate number of the vehicle in front. 
 This was because she wanted to bring a claim against its driver as her back pain had, apparently, immediately worsened. 
 She had even asked Tan to be her witness in this intended claim before she subsequently changed her mind about who she should go after, the judge noted. 
 In addition, the court heard that Chen had at least two other actions that were pending before the District Court. 
 Both involved accidents in which Chen was a passenger. 
 Reasonable brake
 After considering all the points, the judge said that there was "really nothing more" Tan could have been expected to do in the circumstances that confronted him. 
 The force and manner of his braking did not exceed what was reasonably necessary to avoid a collision, he noted. 
 He ultimately found that Tan was not responsible for the incident and dismissed Chen's claim. 
 Chen was ordered to pay Tan S$15,000 in costs.
